description: Before the 2013 mass closures, Chicago Public Schools closed six schools at the end of the 2011-12 school year using a new "utilization formula" developed by CEO Jean-Claude Brizard (who preceded Byrd-Bennett). The closures were accompanied by controversial decisions to co-locate charter schools in existing CPS buildings, sparking community protests. The district also released data showing 140 schools were "underutilized," building the analytical framework that Byrd-Bennett would later use to justify the far larger 2013 closure wave. The 2012 closures, combined with the contentious 2012 Chicago Teachers Union strike over school closures and evaluations, set the stage for the largest mass closure in US history the following year.

title: DCPS Chancellor Rhee Closes 23 Schools Under Mayor Fenty
schools_affected: 23 public schools closed across DC
description: In 2008, DCPS Chancellor Michelle Rhee, appointed by Mayor Adrian Fenty, closed 23 public schools in a major consolidation effort driven by declining enrollment and the need to modernize remaining facilities. The closures, concentrated in lower-income communities east of Rock Creek Park, displaced thousands of students and sparked significant community opposition. Rhee's aggressive reform agenda, which included the closures alongside controversial teacher evaluation and dismissal policies, became a flashpoint in national education reform debates. The 2008 closures set the precedent for Chancellor Henderson's 2013 round of 15 additional closures. Together, the two rounds eliminated approximately 38 schools from the DCPS portfolio in five years.

title: Pittsburgh Implements Right-Sizing Plan with Staff Cuts and School Changes
schools_affected: Multiple schools affected by restructuring
description: In 2006, Pittsburgh Public Schools implemented a comprehensive Right-Sizing Plan that eliminated 252 staffing positions across administrators, teachers, paraprofessionals, clerical staff, and custodians. The plan restructured school feeder patterns, changed the instructional model to emphasize universal access to art, music, and physical education, and increased class sizes. The Right-Sizing Plan was the first major attempt to address the fundamental mismatch between PPS's building capacity (designed for 40,000 students) and actual enrollment (approximately 25,000 at the time, declining to 18,000 by 2024). The 2006 plan set the template for the 2011 Realignment Plan and 2012 closures that followed.

title: KCPS Reopens Hale Cook Elementary Through Grassroots Community Effort
schools_affected: Hale Cook Elementary School
description: In August 2014, Kansas City Public Schools reopened Hale Cook Elementary School at 7302 Pennsylvania Ave. in the Brookside neighborhood, four years after it was mothballed during the 2010 mass closures. The reopening was driven by the grassroots "Friends of Hale Cook" community organization, which mobilized neighborhood support to convince the district to reopen the school. Hale Cook launched with 108 students in pre-K through 2nd grade. The successful community-led reopening became a rare positive counterpoint to the wave of school closures occurring nationwide, demonstrating that engaged communities could reverse closure decisions and rebuild neighborhood schools.

title: Michigan Creates Education Achievement Authority - Takes Over 15 DPS Schools
schools_affected: 15 lowest-performing Detroit schools transferred to state EAA
description: As part of Emergency Manager Roy Roberts' 2012 restructuring of Detroit Public Schools, 15 of the district's lowest-performing schools were transferred to the newly created Education Achievement Authority (EAA), a statewide district designed to turn around failing schools. The EAA was jointly governed by the state and Eastern Michigan University. The transferred schools were placed under separate administration with new curricula and technology-focused learning models. However, the EAA was widely criticized for poor outcomes, with test scores remaining among the lowest in the state. The EAA was eventually dissolved and its schools returned to Detroit Public Schools Community District control. The experiment was seen as a cautionary tale about state-run turnaround districts that removed schools from local democratic governance.

title: 11 Atlanta Educators Convicted on RICO Charges in Cheating Scandal
schools_affected: District-wide impact on accountability and governance
description: On April 1, 2015, after the longest criminal trial in Georgia history (8 months, beginning September 29, 2014), 11 of 12 remaining defendants were convicted on racketeering charges under Georgia's RICO Act. The convicted educators included three executive administrators, one principal, one assistant principal, four teachers, and two testing coordinators. Lead prosecutor Fani Willis secured the convictions. The trial revealed systematic cheating including "cheating parties," classroom erasure sessions, and directives from administrators to alter student test answers. The convictions cemented the Atlanta cheating scandal as the largest standardized test cheating case in American history. Under new Superintendent Maria Carstarphen, APS implemented comprehensive ethics training, replaced leadership at affected schools, and undertook a "child-centered agenda" to rebuild public trust. The scandal revealed how high-stakes testing accountability pressures, including the threat of school closures for poor performance, could incentivize widespread fraud.

title: Baltimore 21st Century Schools Year 1 Construction Begins on 11 Schools
schools_affected: 2 replacement school buildings; 9 renovation projects; 11 total Year 1 schools
description: Construction began on Year 1 of the Baltimore 21st Century Schools Buildings Program, with 11 schools receiving major work — 2 complete replacements and 9 comprehensive renovations. The nearly $1 billion program, a partnership between Baltimore City Public Schools, the Maryland Stadium Authority, Baltimore City, and the State of Maryland, represented the most significant investment in Baltimore school infrastructure in decades. Each school project was paired with an INSPIRE neighborhood improvement plan covering a quarter-mile radius around the school. The Year 2 Request for Qualification process for 17 additional schools began in late Fall 2015. The program aimed to be substantially completed by 2021, ultimately delivering 29 renovated or replaced school buildings.

title: MPS Commissions Long-Range Facilities Master Plan Study
schools_affected: District-wide assessment of 149 school buildings
causes: charter_competition; enrollment_decline; facility_condition; political_governance; population_growth; underutilization
description: In 2017, Milwaukee Public Schools hired MGT of America Consulting to create a long-term facilities master plan, acknowledging the growing crisis of aging infrastructure and declining enrollment. MPS buildings averaged over 80 years old, with only 21 schools built after 1970. The district had reduced from 178 schools in 2008 to 149 but still had approximately one quarter of schools underutilized and another quarter overcrowded. Enrollment had dropped by 30,000 students since 2006, driven significantly by Wisconsin's voucher program and charter school expansion. The study set the stage for eventual recommendations to close or merge 13 additional schools, though those recommendations would not be acted upon until 2024. The delay between study and action reflected the political difficulty of closing schools in predominantly low-income, minority communities.

title: California Takes Over Oakland Unified After $82M Deficit
schools_affected: All OUSD schools (district-wide governance change)
description: In 2003, the State of California took control of Oakland Unified School District after the district accumulated an $82 million deficit. The state provided a $100 million emergency loan and installed a state administrator, removing the elected school board's governing authority. The takeover lasted until 2009, during which time the state administrator oversaw budget cuts, school closures, and the expansion of charter schools in Oakland. The experience shaped OUSD's subsequent facility decisions for years, including the 2012 closures and later rounds. The district's financial struggles, combined with rapid charter school growth, created ongoing tension over facilities, enrollment, and the equitable distribution of resources between traditional public schools and charters — a dynamic that persists to this day.

title: CPS Faces Fiscal Crisis with $1B+ Annual Deficits and Junk Bond Rating
schools_affected: All CPS schools (district-wide fiscal impact)
description: By 2015, Chicago Public Schools was deep in a fiscal crisis with annual budget deficits exceeding $1 billion, driven by pension obligations, declining enrollment, and rising debt service costs. Moody's downgraded CPS debt to junk status, making the district the largest school system in the country with a junk bond rating. The fiscal pressure that had driven the 2013 mass closures continued unabated, with the district's pension fund only 52% funded. CPS increasingly relied on short-term borrowing at unfavorable rates to make ends meet. The financial crisis constrained capital investment in school buildings, deferred maintenance across the district's 600+ facilities, and created ongoing tension between the district, the Chicago Teachers Union, and state lawmakers over funding reform.

district: Shelby County Schools / Achievement School District
title: Tennessee Achievement School District Expands in Memphis
schools_affected: Multiple low-performing Memphis schools transferred to ASD
description: The Tennessee Achievement School District (ASD), created in 2010 to take over the state's lowest-performing schools (bottom 5%), expanded its presence in Memphis following the 2013 merger. The ASD converted failing traditional public schools to charter management, aiming to move them from the bottom 5% to the top 25% within five years. The program was part of Tennessee's broader education reform strategy but faced criticism for removing schools from local democratic control and disproportionately affecting communities of color in Memphis. The ASD's track record was mixed — while some schools showed improvement, many fell short of the ambitious targets. The expansion coincided with the already turbulent merger period, adding another layer of complexity to Memphis-Shelby County's education landscape.

title: DPS Closes Zerger Elementary as Part of Portfolio Management Model
schools_affected: Zerger Elementary School (closed, later became charter school site)
description: Denver Public Schools closed Zerger Elementary School in 2012 as part of its portfolio management approach to education reform. The building was subsequently used to house a public charter school. Zerger's closure was part of a broader DPS strategy during the 2008-2015 period in which the district opened 65 new schools while closing, replacing, or restarting 35 others. A comprehensive study later found that students who transferred from closed schools to new reform-era schools saw significant academic gains in math, validating the closure-and-replacement model in Denver's context. The portfolio model made Denver a nationally studied example of market-based education reform, though community resistance eventually led to the abandonment of the School Performance Compact policy in 2018.

title: Louisiana Governor Signs Act 91 Mandating New Orleans School Reunification
schools_affected: All 52 RSD charter schools to transfer to OPSB by 2018-2019
description: On May 12, 2016, Governor John Bel Edwards signed SB 432 into law as Act 91, mandating that all Recovery School District schools in New Orleans be returned to the locally elected Orleans Parish School Board by July 1, 2018 (with possible extension to 2019). The legislation preserved charter school autonomy while restoring local democratic oversight. The law was the product of years of advocacy by community leaders who argued that the state takeover, while producing some academic gains, had removed Black community voice from governance of a majority-Black school system. The Orleans Parish School Board approved the unification transition plan in August 2016, beginning an 18-month implementation phase with quarterly milestones and an advisory committee. The legislation specifically prohibited OPSB from impeding charter school operational autonomy, reflecting the political compromise required for passage.

title: DPSCD Facilities Assessment Identifies $500M in Immediate Capital Needs
schools_affected: All DPSCD school buildings assessed
description: A comprehensive facilities assessment conducted in 2018 for the newly reconstituted Detroit Public Schools Community District pegged the district's immediate capital needs at over $500 million, with the potential for costs to grow to $1.5 billion by 2023 if left unaddressed. The assessment highlighted that the 2016 state bailout legislation had focused on operating debt relief but did not provide resources for capital needs. Moody's warned that "mounting capital needs now threaten DPSCD's long-term stability" and suggested the district might need another state bailout. The facilities crisis encompassed deteriorating buildings, inadequate heating and cooling systems, structural deficiencies, and in some cases, environmental hazards. The assessment underscored the lasting infrastructure damage from decades of emergency management, school closures, and deferred maintenance.

schools_affected: 5 new schools; 7 school renovations
description: Wake County voters approved a $530.7 million school bond referendum on November 8, 2022, as part of over $1 billion in bond approvals. The bond funds construction of five new schools (elementary schools in Apex, Fuquay-Varina, and Wendell; a middle school in Morrisville; and a high school serving west Cary/Morrisville) plus major renovations at seven existing schools. Property tax impact was 1 cent per $100 of assessed value. The bond supplements a 7-year building plan (FY 2023-2029) totaling $2.632 billion for 11 new schools and 10 major renovations.

schools_affected: Bowling Road Elementary (Fuquay-Varina); Pleasant Plains Elementary (Apex); Rex Road Elementary (Holly Springs); Felton Grove High School (Apex)
description: Four new schools opened for the 2025-26 school year to address tremendous growth in Southern Wake County. Rex Road Elementary is a 133,000 sq ft campus designed for 800 K-5 students. The four new schools bring the district total to 203 schools serving 161,115+ students. The district forecasts growth to 170,000+ students over the next 10 years, with five more schools planned in that period. In 2021-22, 11% of teaching spaces were in 894 mobile/modular classrooms.

schools_affected: Morrisville High School (Little/Davis Drive site)
description: Morrisville High School is planned to open for the 2027-2028 school year with students in grades 9-10. Prior to that, Wake Early College of Information and Biotechnologies will occupy a portion of the building beginning as early as November 2025. A Parkside Middle School is planned to open no earlier than the 2028-2029 school year.

schools_affected: 30 bond projects across the district
description: Mecklenburg County voters approved a historic $2.5 billion school bond, the largest school bond in North Carolina history. The bond covers 30 projects including new middle schools in Huntersville, south and southwest Charlotte; a new health-sciences magnet high school in uptown Charlotte; a new regional athletic facility in west Charlotte; and 25 renovation and replacement projects. Funded by a 3-cent property tax increase phased in during 2025, 2028, and 2029. As enrollment growth slows, the bond shifts focus from new construction to replacing existing aging schools.

schools_affected: Billingsville Elementary (renovation); Sedgefield Elementary (renovation to Montessori magnet); Marie G. Davis School (renovation to Montessori 7-12 magnet)
description: The first projects from the 2023 $2.5 billion bond were completed by August 2025. Billingsville and Sedgefield elementaries and Marie G. Davis School were renovated and reopened as Montessori magnet schools, replacing the older Chantilly, Park Road, and J.T. Williams buildings. Sedgefield moved pre-K-2 students into the Dilworth building in August 2024 as part of the transition.

schools_affected: South Mecklenburg High School (replacement of 1958 building)
description: South Mecklenburg High School replacement of a 1958 classroom building is scheduled for completion in August 2027, funded with both 2017 and 2023 bonds. The replacement of North Mecklenburg High School (opened 1951) is the most expensive project at approximately $228.5 million, scheduled for 2028-2030.

schools_affected: New middle school (Stumptown Road, Huntersville)
description: A new middle school on Stumptown Road in Huntersville is scheduled for completion in August 2028. It will relieve crowding in northern schools, allow the district to add magnet seats, and absorb students from Davidson K-8 when that school converts to an elementary school. CMS is also converting several schools: Thomasboro PreK-8 becomes elementary only, University Park Creative Arts becomes a full K-5 arts magnet, and Rea Farms STEAM becomes a full K-8 magnet.

schools_affected: 7 elementary school renovations; 8 elementary school designs; 1 middle school design; 25+ schools (security vestibules)
description: Fairfax County voters approved a $435 million school bond referendum with 67% support on November 7, 2023. Funds support renovation of seven elementary schools, planning/design of eight additional elementary schools and one middle school, three modular relocations, and security vestibule installation at 25+ schools. FCPS maintains a triple-A bond rating, saving taxpayers an estimated $1 billion in financing costs. School facilities are valued at nearly $6.5 billion.

schools_affected: Braddock Elementary; Louise Archer Elementary; Crossfield Elementary; Mosby Woods Elementary; Bonnie Brae Elementary; Cooper Middle School; Falls Church High School
description: Major renovation projects continued across FCPS as part of the FY 2025-29 CIP. Braddock Elementary ($35.6M) and Louise Archer Elementary ($29.4M) renovations were completed. Crossfield, Mosby Woods, and Bonnie Brae elementaries completed or neared completion. Cooper Middle School and Falls Church High School renovations were underway. FCPS operates on a 41-year renovation cycle for its facilities.

schools_affected: Dunn Loring Elementary (new, from administrative center); Silver Line Elementary (new); Western High School (acquisition and renovation)
description: The FY 2027-2031 CIP requires $1.1 billion over five years for renovation, maintenance, and construction. Plans include repurposing the Dunn Loring Administrative Center into a new elementary school to relieve overcrowding in the Dunn Loring/Falls Church/Tysons area, constructing a new Silver Line Elementary, and acquiring and renovating Western High School. Enrollment is expected to decline from ~177,000 to ~171,000 by 2030-31.

schools_affected: Woodbridge Area Elementary School (new)
description: A new elementary school in the Woodbridge area opened for the 2025-26 school year. The district's CIP 2025-2030 was reassessed based on projected enrollment declines, with several projects slated for delay including the 14th high school and Brentsville District High School renovations.

schools_affected: 14th High School (cancelled)
description: Prince William County officially cancelled plans for its 14th high school, which had been delayed multiple times due to declining enrollment. PWCS data showed the county anticipates 1,030 vacant seats across existing 13 high schools by 2029. The district projects a decrease of approximately 3,776 students over the next five years. Northern Virginia experienced its first population decline since 1970, as residents move to Richmond and exurbs due to housing costs and remote work.

schools_affected: 162 school buildings over 25 years old; 40 HVAC systems not functioning properly
description: MCPS unveiled its "Hard Truths About Our School Buildings" presentation, revealing that nearly two-thirds of its 238 school buildings (162 buildings) are more than 25 years old, with $740 million in overdue projects including 40 non-functioning HVAC systems. The district needs $175 million to replace roofs older than 20 years. To reach long-term goals, MCPS would need to renovate 6-7 elementary schools and 3 middle/high schools every year for 20 years; currently averaging only 5 schools per year.

schools_affected: 13 Major Capital Projects (4 HS, 2 MS, 7 ES)
description: The Board of Education accepted a $2.78 billion Capital Improvements Program (FY 2027-2032) targeting aging buildings, critical systems, and infrastructure. Includes 13 Major Capital Projects (four high schools, two middle schools, seven elementary schools) for completion within six years, plus $521.4 million for HVAC/roof replacements and $303.8 million for other infrastructure renewal. County Executive Marc Elrich proposed $2.1 billion for MCPS in the county's $6.6 billion CIP -- a record allocation.

schools_affected: Crown High School (Gaithersburg, new); Charles W. Woodward High School (reopening)
description: Crown High School in Gaithersburg is expected to open in 2027, along with the reopening of Charles W. Woodward High School and an expansion of Damascus High School for the 2027-2028 year. Parents raised concerns about plans to initially use Crown as a "holding school." The openings require comprehensive boundary studies with at least seven options being considered for attendance zone redraws.

schools_affected: Silver Spring International Middle School (proposed closure 2030)
description: The MCPS superintendent proposed closing the 90-year-old Silver Spring International Middle School in 2030 and converting it to a holding school. In December 2025, the school board suspended consideration of the closure, choosing to incorporate the decision into a future holistic study of elementary school boundaries. Enrollment has dropped to a 10-year low, with steeper declines projected due to lower birth rates and fewer international students. The district has not shuttered a campus in decades.

schools_affected: 8 new schools (6 elementary, 2 K-8)
description: PGCPS brought more than $660 million in taxable sustainable revenue bonds to fast-track construction of eight new schools via a public-private partnership (P3) -- the second P3 package for the district but the first using taxable municipal bonds. The eight schools (six elementary and two K-8) comprise 1.03 million sq ft with enrolling capacity of approximately 8,150 students. Prince George's County contributes $69 million annually to the P3 fund.

schools_affected: Eutaw-Marshburn Elementary (West Baltimore); Steuart Hill Academic Academy (Union Square); New Era Academy (South Baltimore)
description: The Baltimore City school board voted to permanently close three public schools during summer 2023, citing low enrollment and deteriorating buildings. A fourth school, Dr. Bernard Harris Elementary, was kept open as its facility issues were less severe. The board also voted unanimously to develop a strategic plan for long-term enrollment and school closures.

schools_affected: Baltimore City College; Frederick Douglass High School; Baltimore Polytechnic Institute; Western High School
description: Baltimore City invested $400 million in renovating its oldest school buildings as part of the 21st Century School Buildings Program successor (Built to Learn Act of 2021). Baltimore City College moved to the former Thurgood Marshall HS building for three years during construction. Frederick Douglass HS moved to Garrison Middle for two years. Polytechnic Institute and Western High were slated to move in 2025 to Northwestern and Chinquapin buildings respectively. The program has delivered 29 new or renovated schools at approximately $40 million each.

schools_affected: Lansdowne High School (new, $26M state funds); Towson High School (renovation, $20M state funds); Deer Park Elementary (new, $15M state funds); Scott's Branch Elementary (new, $10M state funds); Dundalk High School (addition, $8M state funds); Pine Grove Middle School (addition, $1M state funds)
description: Baltimore County received $80 million in additional state grant funds to accelerate major school construction projects. These are part of County Executive Olszewski's $3.3 billion plan to improve every school in Baltimore County over 15 years, including almost $210 million in new spending in 2023. Just under 80% of BCPS school buildings are 40+ years old. The Multi-Year Improvement Plan for All Schools (MYIPAS) was commissioned in 2020 using CannonDesign consultants.

schools_affected: Campfield Early Learning Center (Gwynn Oak)
description: The Baltimore County Board of Education voted on March 11, 2025 to close Campfield Early Learning Center at the end of the current academic year, earlier than the originally planned 2025-26 closure. With fewer than 60 students projected, officials determined students' needs could be better met at home schools or nearby regional programs. The Campfield site was approved in January 2024 as the future location of the Northwest Area Career and Technology Education Center. The original closure was approved by a 6-5 board vote in September 2023.

schools_affected: All GCPS schools (district-wide E-SPLOST continuation)
description: Gwinnett County voters approved continuation of the existing E-SPLOST (Education Special Purpose Local Option Sales Tax) with 76.6% support. Since 1997, E-SPLOST has funded construction of 64 new schools and 101 school additions, plus technology upgrades and classroom modernization. GCPS holds a "Aaa" bond rating from both Moody's and S&P -- one of only two Georgia school districts to do so.

schools_affected: Seckinger High School (new); Jones Middle School (two-story addition)
description: Seckinger High School opened as the biggest highlight of GCPS new facilities for fall 2022. Jones Middle School received a new two-story addition. Both projects were funded by voter-approved E-SPLOST sales tax and bonds from the 2018 GO Bond referendum ($350 million, approved with 78% support), which also funded general building renovations, safety enhancements, and technology upgrades district-wide.

schools_affected: Archer High School (three-story addition); Berkmar High School (cafeteria renovation); North Gwinnett High School (25-classroom addition); Trickum Middle School (25-classroom addition); 13 career and technical lab projects
description: Major summer 2025 construction included a three-story addition at Archer High and cafeteria renovation at Berkmar High. HVAC systems were replaced at seven schools (Bethesda ES, Camp Creek ES, Collins Hill HS, Crews MS, Creekland MS, Harris ES, Northbrook/Buice Centers). 13 career/tech lab projects were completed at Brookwood HS, Archer HS, Dacula HS, Parkview HS, Pinckneyville MS, Shiloh MS, and Maxwell HS of Technology. Murphy Middle School and a 20-classroom wing at Harbins Elementary open August 2026.

schools_affected: Pope High School (facility upgrades); Sprayberry High School (stadium improvements); South Cobb High School (stadium improvements)
description: Ed-SPLOST VI-funded renovations across the district include Pope High School receiving front entry improvements, new flooring, locker removal, and substantial athletic facility upgrades (renovated locker rooms, new baseball restroom/concessions building, field improvements) with completion expected November 2025. Sprayberry and South Cobb High Schools received upgraded grandstands and ADA-compliant stadium improvements by May 2025. Cobb Schools avoids bond financing entirely, relying on Ed-SPLOST's one-penny sales tax and maintaining three Triple-A credit ratings.

schools_affected: District-wide (138 schools)
description: DeKalb County unveiled a "reimagining" plan (student assignment planning) to serve as a roadmap for the next decade. The plan recommended redistricting throughout the county by 2030, consolidation of some elementary schools, creation of K-8 facilities in some areas, and rebuilding other schools with sales tax funds. The district declined from 100,000+ students in 2016 to about 92,000, leaving many buildings under-utilized. The process is expected to take 18 months to two years.

schools_affected: Idlewood Elementary; Austin Elementary (new facility); Dunwoody Cluster elementary schools
description: The Board of Education approved redistricting for Idlewood Elementary on February 10, 2025. A separate redistricting process determined new attendance lines for a new Austin Elementary facility to better balance enrollment across Dunwoody Cluster elementary schools. An earlier process had established lines for a new elementary school in Doraville for the 2020-21 school year to balance enrollment in Chamblee and Cross Keys clusters.

schools_affected: Spalding Drive Charter Elementary (Sandy Springs, opened 1966); Parklane Elementary (East Point, opened 1953)
causes: charter_competition; enrollment_decline; facility_condition; new_construction; political_governance; redistricting_rezoning
description: The Fulton County School Board voted on February 20, 2025 to approve closure and redistricting of Spalding Drive Charter Elementary and Parklane Elementary due to the cost of operations, declining enrollment, and aging buildings. Community forums were held in fall 2024 to explain rationale and draw potential new attendance zones for surrounding schools. The closures and new redistricting plan take effect in the 2025-26 school year. FCS is now one of the only metro Atlanta districts free of bond debt, having made its final bond payment, and relies on SPLOST for construction.

schools_affected: Denver Discovery School; Fairview Elementary School; Math and Science Leadership Academy
description: Denver's school board voted to close three schools at the end of the 2022-23 school year after a contentious process that initially proposed 10 closures. The three schools had "critically low enrollment." Of the closed buildings, two were in shared buildings still occupied by other schools; Fairview Elementary was repurposed as a special education program (Next Steps by Chancelight). Enrollment had declined from 86,949 in 2019 to 82,997 in 2022.

schools_affected: 7 schools closed; 3 schools partially closed (grade restructure)
description: The Denver school board voted to shutter seven schools and shrink three more at the end of the 2024-25 school year. The closures eliminate nearly 4,000 vacant seats and save $6.6 million annually. The changes affect 1,087 students (~1% of ~90,000 enrollment). Students of color and low-income families are disproportionately impacted -- seven of 10 schools serve higher percentages of students of color than the district average. Partial closures: Kunsmiller Creative Arts Academy loses elementary grades; Dora Moore ECE-8 loses middle school grades; Denver Center for International Studies loses high school grades.

schools_affected: Palmer Elementary (converted to preschool center); Columbian Elementary (reuse pending); 3 other closed buildings (reuse pending)
description: Denver Public Schools announced repurposing plans for closed elementary buildings. Palmer Elementary at 995 Grape St. will become a preschool center for 2025-26, expanding from three to four preschool classrooms. Plans for Columbian Elementary and other closed buildings remain undetermined. Repurposing funds come from a separate bond measure Denver voters approved in 2024 earmarked for school reconfigurations. The district is managing multiple vacant properties, including Rosedale Elementary (leased to Catholic Archdiocese in 2021, now St. John Paul the Great HS).

schools_affected: 2 new elementary schools (RidgeGate and Sterling Ranch); Sierra Middle School (expansion); All schools (safety/security updates)
description: Douglas County voters approved a $490 million bond (Ballot Issue 5A) with 59% support -- after rejecting a bond request in 2023. The bond allocates $150 million for new school construction in RidgeGate and Sterling Ranch and expansion of Sierra Middle School; $178.9 million for capital renewal and replacement; and $38.2 million for career and technical education (CTE) programs. No property tax increase required -- the district will restructure debt to maintain the current 5.2 mill tax rate. This is the seventh bond since 1984, and the largest since a $250 million package in 2018. More than 62,000 students attend 90 schools.

schools_affected: Emory Elementary; Peck Elementary; Thomson Elementary; Campbell Elementary; Peiffer Elementary; Colorow Elementary; Green Mountain Elementary; Bergen Meadow K-2; Molholm Elementary; Glennon Heights Elementary; Parr Elementary; Sheridan Green Elementary; Witt Elementary; Vivian Elementary; Wilmore Davis Elementary; Kullerstrand Elementary
description: The Jeffco Board of Education voted unanimously on November 10, 2022 to close 16 elementary schools -- the largest mass closure in the district's history. Enrollment dropped from 87,700 in 2000 to 77,205 by fall 2022, with capacity for 96,000 students across 157 schools. The closures affected 2,400+ children and 422 full-time employees. The district faced a budget deficit and had drawn $32 million from reserves. Closures were expected to save up to $12 million annually. Criteria required enrollment below 220 students or capacity utilization below 45%.

schools_affected: Coal Creek Canyon K-8; Arvada K-8; Moore Middle School (consolidated with Pomona HS to become Jr/Sr HS)
description: The school board voted to close two additional K-8 schools and consolidate a middle school, bringing total closures to 21 since 2021. Coal Creek Canyon K-8 was the lowest-enrolled school with fewer than 85 students (45% decline since 2019). Arvada K-8 used only 60% capacity with fewer than 560 students. Moore Middle was consolidated with Pomona High to create Pomona Jr/Sr High (grades 6-12). Jefferson Academy was authorized to open a replication site in the Coal Creek Canyon building.

schools_affected: Jefferson Jr./Sr. High School (Edgewater, proposed transition)
description: Jeffco began considering closing Jefferson Jr./Sr. High School (grades 7-12) and converting it into a specialized career-focused high school. A boundary study found the school unsustainable with projected enrollment of only 372 students by 2027-28 -- with 47% of boundary families already choosing other schools. The district frames it as a "transition" rather than closure, though board members noted it "sounds a lot like closing a school." The district manages 22 closed school properties, with maintenance costing ~$150,000 per year per building. Eight properties found new owners; 14 remain unsold.

schools_affected: 20 new schools built; 37 classroom additions; 18 replacement schools; 82 modernization projects
description: By mid-2021, the 2015 Capital Improvement Program (authorized through Senate Bills 119 and 207) had completed or begun dozens of projects including 20 new schools, 37 classroom additions, 18 replacement schools, five phased replacement schools, and 82 modernization projects. The original 10-year program estimated at $4.1 billion was later extended through 2035 by the state Legislature. The school board gave final approval for $3.5 billion in facility projects for the next 14 years.

schools_affected: 10 schools (construction paused); 125 aging facilities under review
description: CCSD Trustees voted unanimously to pause construction on 10 schools for one year due to project bids increasing 60% and material costs rising 40%. Paused projects include Indian Springs and Cashman Middle School, Northwest Comprehensive High School, and Southeast Choice High School. The district has 125 schools classified as "aging facilities" and projects losing 3,600 students annually. The district needs $15.3 billion in capital bonds but has only $7.3 billion available. CannonDesign was hired for $5 million to assess all school facilities. A Facility Master Plan with closure/reuse recommendations is expected in early 2026.

district: Nevada State Public Charter School Authority
schools_affected: 6 CCSD charter schools absorbed; 5 new charter schools opening 2025-26; 80 charter school campuses statewide
description: The SPCSA expanded significantly, absorbing six Clark County School District-run charter schools in January 2025 (marking CCSD's complete exit from charter school operation) and planning five new charter school openings for 2025-26. Total enrollment surpassed the Washoe County School District, reaching ~69,000 students with projections above 70,000. The expansion adds over 8,000 students, positioning SPCSA as Nevada's second-largest local education agency. 79% of new campuses opened in the last five years are Title I schools. SPCSA schools have an 83.3% graduation rate, with 26 of 27 high schools exceeding the statewide rate.

district: Nevada State Public Charter School Authority
schools_affected: All Nevada public schools including charters
description: The Nevada Legislature passed SB500 securing $12.9 billion for K-12 funding (2025-27 biennium), providing historic investment levels. AB398 allocated $128 million for teacher raises including charter school teachers (previously excluded). SB468 allocated $7 million for charter school student transportation. Cities of Henderson and North Las Vegas were approved as new charter school authorizers under Gov. Lombardo's Assembly Bill 400, allowing municipalities to sponsor and oversee charter schools within their boundaries.

title: Two New Schools Open for 2023-24
schools_affected: Richard A. Wilkinson Middle School; Shana K. Wortham Intermediate
description: Frisco ISD opened two new schools for the 2023-24 school year, bringing the district total to 77 campuses. Wortham Intermediate was the first of its kind in the district, serving 5th and 6th graders. The openings came as seven campuses were already at capacity, including four elementary and three middle schools.

title: VATRE Rejected; District Shifts to Open Enrollment
schools_affected: District-wide (77 campuses)
description: Frisco ISD voters rejected a Voter Approval Tax Rate Election (VATRE) with 57.45% voting against. The district faced a $30.8 million budget shortfall for 2024-25. In response, the district launched the "Access Frisco" program to open enrollment to K-7 students from surrounding areas in 2025-26, seeking $750,000 in state funding per 100 additional students to compensate for plateauing local growth.

title: $698 Million Bond Approved
schools_affected: District-wide (42+ schools, 40,000+ students)
description: Leander ISD voters approved all three propositions of the 2023 bond election. Proposition A authorized $698.3 million for school facilities, including three new schools (Elementary Schools 31 and 32 and High School 7), an early childhood center, and modernization projects at Cedar Park HS, Vista Ridge HS, and Running Brushy MS. The bond did not require a tax rate increase due to continued growth in the district's tax base.

title: Hisle Elementary School Opens
schools_affected: Hisle Elementary School (Elementary School 30)
description: Hisle Elementary School, funded by the 2023 bond, opened to students on August 14, 2024, located near Devine Lake Park in the northwest part of the district. The new school provided enrollment relief to overcrowded Bagdad and Plain elementary schools.

title: Three New Schools Open for 2023-24
schools_affected: Christopher J. Hines Elementary; Veterans Memorial Intermediate; Grangerland Intermediate
description: Conroe ISD opened three new campuses for the 2023-24 school year to address overcrowding as enrollment topped 73,000 students. Veterans Memorial Intermediate in Grangerland has a capacity of 1,050 students serving the Caney Creek HS feeder zone. Grangerland Intermediate expanded student capacity to 1,600.

title: $1.8 Billion Bond Approved
schools_affected: District-wide (eight new schools plus eight additions/renovations)
description: Conroe ISD voters approved propositions A, B, and C of a $1.9 billion bond package in November 2023 (Proposition D was rejected). Proposition A set aside $1.8 billion for eight new schools including Timber Mill High School (3,800-student capacity), multiple elementary schools, and junior high schools, plus additions and renovations to existing campuses. The district covers 348 square miles including The Woodlands.

title: $932 Million Bond Approved (Athletics Prop Rejected)
schools_affected: District-wide (average campus age 30 years)
description: Round Rock ISD voters approved $932.2 million in three of four bond propositions on November 5, 2024. Proposition A ($798.3 million) covers maintenance including HVAC, roofing, and plumbing. Voters rejected Prop D for athletic facility upgrades. This was the district's first bond in six years. The bond would actually lower the tax rate by about 2.5 cents due to growth in the tax base. First-year projects include an Early College High School and a new CTE center.

title: Two New K-8 Schools Open
schools_affected: K-8 School (Shearwater community, CR 16A); K-8 School (Beacon Lakes area, CR 210)
description: St. Johns County opened two new K-8 schools in August 2024, each serving about 1,500 students. The district is one of the fastest-growing in Florida with over 600 portable classrooms housing about 13,000 students. At least 10 of 51 schools were over capacity. Each new school cost approximately $68 million to build.

title: Spring Park Elementary Opens
schools_affected: Spring Park Elementary School
description: Clay County's 43rd and newest school, Spring Park Elementary in Green Cove Springs, opened for the 2023-24 school year. The 104,000 square foot prototype school cost over $40 million, includes 48 classrooms, and serves 800+ students in grades K-6. Built on budget, on time, and debt free. The district is forecasting 7,000-10,000 more students over the next decade due to completion of the First Coast Expressway.

title: Five New Schools Planned; K-8 Construction Begins
schools_affected: New K-8 School (Lakewood Ranch, Academic Avenue); New Middle School (North River Ranch); New High School (Lakewood Ranch area, planned 2027); Rye Ranch Elementary (planned 2026); Artisan Lakes Elementary (planned 2026)
description: Manatee County began construction on a $104.6 million K-8 school in Lakewood Ranch with a capacity of 1,620 students, set to open in 2025. The district plans to open five new schools by 2027 to address rapid growth in eastern Manatee County, including a $200 million high school. The district projects 7,077 additional students over the next decade. A new middle school at North River Ranch will cost $68.7 million.

title: $179M New Cherokee High School Approved
schools_affected: Cherokee High School (replacement campus)
description: The Cherokee County School District Board approved construction of a new Cherokee High School campus in May 2023 at a cost of $179 million — the largest contract ever for a CCSD high school. The new campus covers 88 acres and 473,761 square feet, designed for 3,000+ students with 152 classrooms and state-of-the-art CTAE labs. The original campus dates to 1956 and is the oldest and most expensive to maintain in the county. Funded via Ed-SPLOST revenue with $31 million from the state.

title: $120 Million School Bond Approved
schools_affected: District-wide (48 schools, 36,879 students)
description: Johnston County voters approved a $120 million general obligation bond by a 56.75% margin on November 5, 2024. Johnston County is the fastest-growing county in North Carolina and 9th fastest nationally. The district has 167 mobile classrooms and 72% of schools are at or over capacity. Bond proceeds fund new construction, additions/renovations at eight elementary schools, fire panel replacements, and HVAC upgrades. The Board had originally sought $285 million.

title: School Construction Bond Referendum
schools_affected: Parkwood High School (pre-construction for new school); East Union Middle School (relocation to Forest Hills HS campus)
description: Union County Public Schools placed a school construction bond referendum on the November 2024 ballot to invest in pre-construction for a new Parkwood High School and relocate East Union Middle School to the Forest Hills High campus. The bond builds on previous investments to modernize aging schools in one of North Carolina's fastest-growing suburban counties near Charlotte.

title: $325M Bond Rejected by Voters
schools_affected: District-wide
description: Gilbert Public Schools voters rejected a $325 million bond question in November 2023, part of a broader trend in Maricopa County where voters in Gilbert, Mesa ($500M), and Queen Creek ($98M for the third consecutive year) all rejected school bond proposals. 2023 was a record-setting year for Arizona school bond questions, with 23 districts requesting over $3.56 billion statewide. The rejections reflected growing voter skepticism toward school bonds despite facility needs.

title: Infrastructure Bond Measure Rejected
schools_affected: District-wide
description: Chandler USD voters rejected a school infrastructure improvements bond measure in the November 2024 election. The rejection reflects declining enrollment making the district ineligible for Arizona School Facilities Division funds for new schools. Concerns were raised about Chandler taxpayers funding schools physically located in Gilbert (Perry HS) and Queen Creek (Casteel HS) due to the district's geographic expansion across city lines.

title: $475 Million Building Generations Bond
schools_affected: New Elementary School (West Point); New Elementary School (Sunset); Island View Elementary (rebuild)
description: Davis School District voters approved a $475 million "Building Generations" bond to fund new school construction and improvements. Construction in West Point and Sunset was in full swing by June 2023 with steel and concrete walls going up at the new elementary schools. The district, serving students in Davis County north of Salt Lake City, continues to experience growth requiring bonds every two years.

title: New Elementary School in Star Opens
schools_affected: New Elementary School (south of SH-44 in Star)
description: West Ada School District, Idaho's largest (35,000+ students), broke ground on a new elementary school in Star funded by HB 521 facilities funds ($150 million total received by the district). The $20 million school, built for 700 students, gives children south of State Highway 44 a neighborhood school, ending 7-mile bus rides to Eagle. The district projects 11,000 new students over the next decade and plans to seek bonds every two years to keep pace with growth.

title: Board Votes to Close 11 Schools and 5 Buildings
schools_affected: School No. 20; School No. 29; School No. 39; School No. 44; School No. 106; Montessori Academy (School No. 53, relocated); Rochester Early College International HS (relocated); Additional schools (11 total)
causes: charter_competition; covid_pandemic; enrollment_decline; facility_condition; political_governance; underutilization
description: The Rochester City School District Board of Education voted in October 2023 to close 11 schools and vacate five buildings. Superintendent Carmine Peluso cited enrollment declines, poor school performance, building conditions, and projections that the district would fall below 14,000 students within 10 years without action. Rochester kept schools closed for in-person instruction during the pandemic longer than any other NY district besides Buffalo, accelerating enrollment losses to charters and homeschooling.

title: Building Brighter Futures -- 29 Schools Merged, 18 Buildings Close
schools_affected: 29 schools merged (61 elementary to 45; 27 high schools to 14); 18 school buildings closed entirely
description: The CMSD Board unanimously approved the "Building Brighter Futures" consolidation plan to merge 39 schools, reducing by 29, and close 18 buildings. Enrollment dropped from 70,000 in 2004 to 34,000 in 2024, with buildings at half or one-third capacity. The district faces a budget deficit by 2028 without change and needs to save $150 million. The plan saves $30 million/year and affects about 5,000 students for 2026-27. Ohio's expanded voucher and charter programs contributed to enrollment losses.

title: Firestone Park Elementary Closed in Right-Sizing Plan
schools_affected: Firestone Park Elementary School; Essex Early Learning Program (terminated); Stewart Early Learning Program (terminated)
description: The Akron Board of Education approved a redistricting plan that closed Firestone Park Elementary and terminated early learning programs at Essex and Stewart as part of a "right-sizing" effort. Some buildings had less than 50% enrollment, putting them at risk under Ohio law that would put under-used buildings up for sale to charter schools. Four additional buildings are planned for closure in a phased approach through 2027.

title: Historic Phase 2 Restructuring Approved
schools_affected: South Avondale School (becomes middle school); Ethel M. Taylor Academy (becomes junior high); Pleasant Hill Academy (becomes Pleasant Hill Middle School); Riverview East Academy (closed in Phase 1); William H. Taft Elementary (magnet status removed); Sayler Park (expands to K-12); 30 schools total affected by redistricting
description: The Cincinnati Public Schools board approved a sweeping Phase 2 restructuring during a 6.5-hour meeting, moving students at nearly 30 schools and creating six new middle schools. The plan divides the district into three geographical corridors. Phase 1 closed Riverview East Academy. The restructuring addresses a projected $215 million cost and follows declining enrollment patterns. No teacher layoffs are expected.

title: Plan to Close 37 of 68 Schools Proposed
schools_affected: 27 elementary schools; 5 middle schools; 5 high schools
description: Architecture firm Cordogan, Clark & Associates presented a master plan to the St. Louis Public School Board proposing closure of 37 of 68 schools by 2026-27. Enrollment peaked at 115,000 students in 1967 and has fallen to about 18,122. The district has capacity for 30,000+ students. Closures would save $42 million in 2026-27 alone. A May 2025 tornado ($63 million in damage) further complicated the situation, threatening to displace more families from the district.

title: Board Approves Phased Closure of Four Schools
schools_affected: Pierce Elementary (closed 2024-25); Neithercut Elementary (closed 2025-26); Two additional buildings (through 2027)
description: Flint Community Schools Board approved closing four buildings in a phased approach from 2024-2027. Building utilization averaged 55% vs. the state-recommended 85%. With enrollment at 2,823 students, the district maintained nearly 451,000 sq ft of unnecessary space costing $3.6-4.5 million annually. The district carried $56 million in debt and a $14.4 million operational deficit. ESSER funding of $150 million since 2021 ended in September 2024.

title: Reimagine GRPS -- 10 Schools to Close by 2028
schools_affected: East Leonard Elementary (closed 2024); Stocking Elementary (closed 2024); Southeast Career Pathways/Jefferson (closing 2025); Brookside Elementary (closing 2026); Palmer Elementary (closing 2027); Aberdeen Academy (closing 2027); Westwood Middle School (closing 2028); Three additional schools (closing 2025-2026)
description: Grand Rapids Public Schools Board unanimously approved the "Reimagine GRPS" facilities master plan to close 10 school buildings between 2024 and 2028. The closures save $60+ million in maintenance and repair costs for underutilized buildings. Voters approved a $305 million bond in 2023 to improve remaining schools. East Leonard and Stocking Elementary were the first to close at the end of 2023-24.

title: 360 High School Closed and Merged
schools_affected: 360 High School (merged into Juanita Sanchez High School)
description: Providence's 360 High School was closed and merged with Juanita Sanchez High School at the end of the 2023-24 year, creating the Juanita Sanchez Life Sciences Institute. Superintendent Montanez cited decreased enrollment making it "increasingly difficult to provide equitable opportunities in smaller high schools." Parents sued to block the closure, arguing it violated the Equal Educational Opportunity Act by harming Spanish-speaking students. Students protested inside the school. The district has been under state control since 2019.

title: Five-School Closure Proposal Rejected
schools_affected: Five schools identified (not named publicly before rejection)
description: Richmond School Board Member Jonathan Young proposed closing five schools to save $5 million, citing 8,600 vacant seats across the district. The proposal failed in February 2023 after opposition from board members, parents, and the Richmond NAACP, who questioned the equity of closing schools in predominantly African American neighborhoods. Board member Kenya Gibson stated "I do not support any school closures."

title: Efficiency Initiative Launched to Close 10 Schools
schools_affected: Ghent School; Tarrallton Elementary; Willoughby Early Childhood Center; Norview Elementary; Oceanair Elementary (repurposed); Five additional schools (through 2034)
description: Norfolk Public Schools launched an efficiency and modernization initiative targeting 10 school closures after enrollment fell from 32,000 (2014-15) to 26,000. A consultant found the district operated 3-17 more schools than necessary since 2013, wasting an estimated $81 million. City Council requested an action plan by 2026-27. The Board voted 6-1 in October 2025 to close 9 schools by 2033-34 under the Consolidation and Equity Transition Plan.

title: Supreme Court Upholds Act 46 Forced Mergers
schools_affected: 120+ districts statewide (reduced from 276 pre-merger)
description: The Vermont Supreme Court narrowly ruled against school districts fighting forced mergers under Act 46, upholding the state-imposed consolidation that reduced districts from 276 to 120 and eliminated over 150 school boards. 63% of K-12 students live in new union districts. However, a Yale study found no significant savings in per-pupil spending — savings were absorbed by higher salaries and busing costs. Some communities like Halifax-Readsboro successfully demerged.

title: Kansas' Smallest District Plans Dissolution
schools_affected: Healy School (estimated 19 students)
description: Healy USD 468, Kansas' smallest school district with an estimated 19 students in grades 5-8, developed a plan to dissolve and consolidate after years of declining enrollment. Eight other K-12 districts in Kansas have fewer than 100 students and 28 have fewer than 200. The state has no blueprint for dealing with dissolution. The case caught lawmakers' attention as a harbinger of broader rural decline.

title: Disorganization Vote After High School Closure
schools_affected: Wilson High School (73 students, 50% decline over 10 years)
description: Barton County residents voted on August 1, 2023, on whether to disorganize USD 112 after the closure of Wilson's high school, which had seen a 50% enrollment decline over 10 years. The vote was described as "brand new territory" for the Kansas Department of Education and State Board. The Wetmore community also faced its third school closure in 10 years, highlighting the cascading impact on rural communities.

title: Two Rural Districts Vote to Consolidate
schools_affected: Oldham-Ramona School; Rutland School; New K-12 school (planned on Highway 81)
description: The Oldham-Ramona and Rutland school districts in Kingsbury, Miner, Lake, Moody, and Brookings counties voted to consolidate in 2022, planning to build a new K-12 school along Highway 81 for all students by 2025-26. The consolidation was projected to reduce combined operational costs from $4 million to $3 million. The merger reflects ongoing rural South Dakota population decline.

title: State Board Approves Closures Across Six Counties
schools_affected: Clay County Middle School (consolidated); Fellowsville Elementary (Preston County, merged into South Preston); Rowlesburg School (Preston County, merged into Aurora); Hundred High School (Wetzel County, merged into Valley HS); Paden City High School (Wetzel County, merged into Magnolia HS); Belle Elementary (Kanawha County); Malden Elementary (Kanawha County); Mary Ingles Elementary (Kanawha County); Midland Trail Elementary (Kanawha County)
description: The West Virginia Board of Education approved school closures across Clay, Preston, Wetzel, and Kanawha counties in December 2024. Fifty-three schools closed in the prior five years, with 25 more proposed in 2024. Clay County lost nearly a third of enrolled students in under 10 years. Fellowsville Elementary saw 50.8% enrollment decline over a decade. The Hope Scholarship voucher program (10,000+ students) and charter expansion (2,277 students) accelerated public school enrollment losses.

title: Board Votes to Close 13 Schools
schools_affected: Obama Elementary (consolidated with Northwest IB); Wells APAC Elementary (consolidated with Bailey APAC); 11 additional schools closed or consolidated
description: The Jackson Public Schools Board voted 5-1 to close or consolidate 13 schools effective for the 2024-25 school year after months of community forums. JPS lost about 10,000 students and had 400+ staffing vacancies over the prior decade. The plan saves $17+ million annually and $174 million in renovation costs. State Rep. Chris Bell supported the plan to avoid renewed state takeover due to financial distress. Initial proposal targeted 16 schools but was reduced.

title: $480 Million Bond Approved After 20-Year Drought
schools_affected: District-wide (87 schools, 40,000+ students, average building age 55 years)
description: Tucson Unified voters approved a $480 million bond by a 59-41% margin in November 2023, breaking a 20-year bond drought (last passed in 2004; a 2017 attempt failed). Funds cover $263.9M for facility upgrades, $75.5M for security and safety, $66.4M for technology, $43M for classroom improvements, and $31.2M for transportation. Rincon/University HS receives the most funding (~$16M). Average school age is 55 years, with some buildings over 100 years old.

title: Board Votes 4-3 to Close 8 Elementary Schools
schools_affected: Carlos Rivera Elementary (closing 2025-26); Lamar Elementary (closing 2025-26); Newman Elementary (closing 2025-26); Putnam Elementary (closing 2025-26); Rusk Elementary (closing 2025-26); Zavala Elementary (closing 2025-26); Travis Elementary (closing 2026-27); Stanton Elementary (closing 2026-27)
description: El Paso ISD Board voted 4-3 to close eight elementary schools during a 5.5-hour meeting in November 2024 under the "Destination District Redesign" plan. The district faces a $32.2 million budget deficit; closures reduce it by nearly 66%. Children born in El Paso County in 2023 were 21% fewer than in 2013. EPISD had already closed nine elementary schools between 2018-21. U.S. Rep. Veronica Escobar called for delay, with her office receiving 1,200+ constituent messages opposing the closures.

title: Board Votes to Close Six Schools
schools_affected: Hadley Middle School; Jardine STEM and Career Exploration Academy; Clark Elementary; Cleaveland Traditional Magnet Elementary; Payne Elementary; Park Elementary
description: Wichita Public Schools Board voted 5-2 to close two middle schools and four elementary schools to address a $42 million budget gap caused by declining enrollment (a trend since 2016 worsened by COVID-19), the end of pandemic relief funding, and building maintenance needs. The closures save about $16 million. Average elementary enrollment was 380 students versus the 600 needed to run at district standards. A subsequent $450 million bond proposal was narrowly defeated in February 2025.

title: State Board Urges School Closures for Low-Performing Sites
schools_affected: Multiple low-performing sites (not yet specified)
description: Oklahoma State Superintendent Ryan Walters and the State Board of Education called for Tulsa Public Schools to identify low-performing school sites for closure during mandatory monthly status updates. Interim Superintendent Ebony Johnson confirmed closures were under consideration as part of a broader consolidation effort. State officials analyzed TPS staffing data and school sizes. TPS stated any closures would be "a local decision" requiring board approval.

title: Bluestem Middle School Opens
schools_affected: Bluestem Middle School
description: Omaha Public Schools opened Bluestem Middle School in August 2023, the fifth and final new school built under the district's $409.9 million Phase 2 bond (approved 2018). The $48.8 million school at 5910 S. 42nd St. opened with 6th and 7th graders, adding 8th grade in 2024. All five new Phase 2 schools totaling nearly $270 million were completed on time and within budget, including Buena Vista HS, Westview HS, Forest Station ES, and Pine ES (opened 2022).

title: Reimagining Education Plan -- Three Schools Close
schools_affected: Howe Elementary; Walnut Street Elementary; Harding Middle School
description: Des Moines Public Schools unveiled the "Reimagining Education" 10-year plan to address 2,200+ student enrollment decline over seven years, aging buildings, and loss of pandemic funding. The revised plan scaled back closures from seven to three schools (Howe ES, Walnut Street ES, and Harding MS) with a $265 million price tag, down from $500 million. The plan also expands full-day preschool and creates eight "signature schools." A $265 million bond passed in November 2025.

title: Three Schools Close at End of 2023-24
schools_affected: Baseline Academy (elementary); Cloverdale Middle School; West High School of Innovation
description: Three Little Rock School District campuses closed at the end of the 2023-24 school year as the district addressed declining enrollment (about 19,000 students for 23,000 seats). The Arkansas LEARNS Act (2023) allowed districts in financial distress to be taken over by charter companies, creating urgency to cut costs. In December 2024, the board further voted 5-4 to merge Carver Elementary with Washington Elementary and relocate Brady Elementary students.

title: Board Approves Additional Elementary Consolidations
schools_affected: Carver Elementary (merged with Washington Elementary); Brady Elementary (students relocated district-wide)
description: The Little Rock School Board voted 5-4 in December 2024 to consolidate more elementary schools, merging Carver and Washington Elementary into Washington Carver Elementary and relocating Brady Elementary students across the district. The consolidations save up to $3 million. The Brady building will become a Parent Center with registration and special education offices. Board member Bolley opposed, saying closing schools "destroyed intentional communities."

title: $170 Million Bond Issuance for Capital Improvements
schools_affected: District-wide (77,000+ students, 11 accelerated improvement projects)
description: The School District of Greenville County, South Carolina's largest district (77,000+ students, 809 sq mi), issued $170 million in general obligation bonds in September 2023 to finance capital improvements, rated MIG 1 by Moody's and A-1+ by S&P. The Long-Range Facilities Plan was updated to accelerate 11 school improvement projects. Since 2001, the district has built or begun 38 new schools and renovated 19, while Greenville County's population grew by nearly 40%.

title: Five Connecticut Schools Close in 2023
schools_affected: Two Mansfield elementary schools (consolidated into one); Three additional schools across the state
description: Five Connecticut schools closed in 2023, including two Mansfield elementary schools consolidated into one. The state has closed 75+ public schools over the past decade while losing 36,000 students (from 550,000 to 513,000 enrollment). Most closures have occurred in areas with large populations of students of color, including Hartford and New Haven. At least 81 schools statewide require some kind of transition before the fifth grade.

title: TEA State Takeover
schools_affected: All 270+ HISD campuses
description: TEA formally took over Houston ISD, replacing the elected school board with an appointed Board of Managers and installing Mike Miles (former Dallas ISD superintendent) as superintendent. The takeover was triggered by Wheatley High School receiving five consecutive F ratings under state accountability. At the time, HISD had a B+ accountability rating overall and a AAA bond rating.

title: New Education System (NES) -- Phase 1 Restructuring
schools_affected: 28 campuses in Wheatley, Kashmere, and North Forest HS feeder patterns (including Kashmere HS, Wheatley HS, North Forest HS, Highland Heights ES, Henry MS, Sugar Grove Academy, Marshall ES, and others)
description: Superintendent Miles launched the NES at 28 historically underperforming campuses. All staff were required to reapply for positions. Schools adopted extended 6:30 AM to 5 PM schedules, new curricula, and centralized budget management. Libraries were converted to "TEAMS centers." An additional 57 schools voluntarily joined as "NES-Aligned" campuses.

title: NES Expansion -- Phase 2
schools_affected: 45 additional campuses (including Austin High School and 18 elementary/middle schools), bringing total to 130 NES campuses
description: HISD expanded NES to 45 more schools, 26 of which were required to join based on failing state ratings and 19 that joined voluntarily. This brought the total NES footprint to 130 campuses -- nearly half the district.

title: $4.4 Billion Bond Rejected
schools_affected: District-wide (would have funded repairs/rebuilds across all campuses)
description: Houston voters overwhelmingly rejected HISD's $4.4 billion bond proposal (Prop A: $3.96B for facilities; Prop B: $440M for technology) by a 58-42% margin. It was the largest school bond in Texas history and the first $1B+ Texas school bond to fail. Both Democratic and Republican parties opposed it under the slogan "No Trust, No Bond," viewing it as a referendum on the state-appointed leadership. Miles estimated the district needs $10B in repairs.

title: School Closures Proposed Then Reversed
schools_affected: Up to 10 unspecified "small" campuses
description: At convocation, Miles announced he would propose closing up to 10 small schools due to declining enrollment (30,000 students lost in 10 years). Each closure would save approximately $2M/year. However, in November 2025, the district reversed course and announced no closures for the 2026-27 school year, though "consolidations" may be considered later.

title: TEA Takeover Extended to 2027
schools_affected: District-wide
description: TEA Commissioner Mike Morath extended state control of HISD until at least June 1, 2027. Three criteria must be met for a return to local control: no campuses failing for multiple consecutive years, special education compliance, and the board demonstrating proper governance.

title: $100M Infrastructure Spending from General Fund
schools_affected: District-wide
description: After the bond failure, HISD announced it would budget $100 million from its general fund for building updates and infrastructure over two years, reducing funds available for salaries and operations. The district faces a projected $250M budget deficit.

title: $3.47 Billion Bond Approved
schools_affected: 200+ campuses
description: Voters approved Proposition A ($3.2B for school construction, renovation, and equipment at 200+ of 230 campuses) and Proposition B ($270M for technology). Three other propositions for sports stadiums, performing arts, and swimming pools were rejected. The bond funds 14 new or replacement campuses.

title: Geneva Heights Elementary Replacement Campus
schools_affected: Geneva Heights Elementary
description: A $31 million replacement campus for Geneva Heights Elementary, with a capacity of 750 students, was constructed as part of the 2020 bond program. It retained a portion of the original building.

title: Three New Schools Opened
schools_affected: Three new campuses (including replacements)
description: Dallas ISD opened the doors of three new schools funded by the 2020 bond program, marking a milestone in the district's facilities transformation.

title: John Quincy Adams and George Peabody Elementary Dedications
schools_affected: John Quincy Adams Elementary, George Peabody Elementary
description: Two replacement campuses -- John Quincy Adams Elementary (unveiled Nov. 14, 2024) and George Peabody Elementary (dedicated Nov. 13, 2024) -- opened as state-of-the-art facilities funded by the 2020 bond.

title: John Lewis Social Justice Academy at O.W. Holmes
schools_affected: O.W. Holmes campus (Southern Dallas)
description: An $80 million investment for the first new campus built in the southern Dallas community in years, part of the 2020 bond addressing historical inequities.

title: Proposed $6.2 Billion Bond for 2026
schools_affected: District-wide; would rebuild 26 campuses and consolidate 2 pairs of schools
description: Dallas ISD staff presented a preliminary $6.2B bond plan for 2026 covering replacement of 26 schools, technology/security upgrades, 500 new buses, and consolidation of Piedmont G.L.O.B.A.L. Academy with San Jacinto ES, and Dr. Frederick Douglass Todd Sr. MS with Whitney M. Young Jr. ES. A Citizens Bond Steering Committee was formed in February 2025.

title: Board Redistricting (Trustee Districts)
schools_affected: District governance
description: Following 2020 Census data, Dallas ISD redrew its Single Member District (trustee) boundaries, holding 35+ community meetings and two TeleTown Halls. The new map was used for the May 2024 elections.

title: $1.2 Billion Bond Narrowly Approved
schools_affected: All middle schools + 4 new elementary schools
description: Proposition A ($1.211B) for school construction and renovation passed by just 42 votes (12,342 to 12,300). It funds major interior renovations to all middle schools and construction of four new elementary schools. Propositions B (Fine Arts, $98.3M), C (Stadiums, $104.9M), and D (Recreation, $76.2M) all failed.

title: Forest Oak Sixth Grade Closed
schools_affected: Forest Oak Sixth Grade
description: Closed due to struggling academic outcomes and state accountability concerns. Forest Oak had earned five consecutive F ratings, putting the district at risk of TEA intervention.

title: Wedgwood Sixth Grade Closed
schools_affected: Wedgwood Sixth Grade
description: Closed due to declining enrollment and underutilization.

title: S.S. Dillow and Eastern Hills Elementary Closures Approved
schools_affected: S.S. Dillow Elementary, Eastern Hills Elementary
description: Board approved closure of both campuses due to declining enrollment and underutilization.

date: August 2024 (McLean approved); December 2024 (West Handley rezoning approved, closes by 2028)
title: McLean 6th Grade and West Handley Elementary Closures
schools_affected: McLean Sixth Grade Center, West Handley Elementary
description: McLean 6th Grade approved for closure in August. West Handley Elementary was effectively closed through an attendance boundary rezoning vote in December.

title: 18-Campus Five-Year Closure Plan Approved
schools_affected: 18 campuses total (4 previously approved + 14 new), including Kirkpatrick ES, H.V. Helbing ES, Riverside Applied Learning Center, Charles E. Nash ES, Atwood McDonald ES, Sunrise-McMillan ES, A.M. Pate ES, Harlean Beal ES, Morningside MS, Edward J. Briscoe ES, Hubbard Heights ES, J.T. Stevens ES, De Zavala ES, and Kirkpatrick MS
description: The board unanimously approved a five-year plan to close 18 campuses (15 elementary, 1 sixth-grade center, 2 middle schools), saving $77.3 million. Closures begin June 2025 and run through June 2029. Community opposition was strong, with 100+ parents packing the meeting. Notably, De Zavala ES had an A rating from TEA.

title: Western Hills Primary Closure
schools_affected: Western Hills Primary (consolidating with Western Hills Elementary)
description: Board voted to consolidate Western Hills Primary with Western Hills Elementary on the same property for the 2026-27 school year. Attendance zones will not change.

title: Bond-Funded Middle School Renovations
schools_affected: 7 middle schools including Wedgwood MS ($46.8M) and Meadowbrook MS ($36.8M)
description: The board approved over $223.5 million in construction contracts for seven middle school renovations as part of the 2021 bond program. Projects include new secured entry vestibules, upgraded corridors, science labs, and removal of portable buildings.

title: $1.76 Billion Bond (Approved 2019, Projects 2020--2024)
schools_affected: District-wide (new schools, renovations, technology, transportation)
description: Voters approved $1.76B for new school construction ($238M technology, $968M facility renovations, $88M transportation). The bond funded the opening of several new campuses through 2024.

title: Rowe Middle School Opened
schools_affected: Rowe Middle School (new campus)
description: New middle school opened as part of the 2019 bond program.

title: Fiest Elementary Renovated
schools_affected: Fiest Elementary School
description: Ribbon-cutting ceremony on Aug. 16, 2021 for the newly renovated campus, part of the 2019 bond's Phase 1 renovations.

title: Dr. Carla Brosnahan Elementary (ES #58) Opened
schools_affected: Dr. Carla Brosnahan Elementary School (Elementary #58)
description: New $33.2 million elementary school opened at 20220 Clay Road in Katy for the 2023-24 school year.

title: Roy J. Sprague Jr. Middle School (MS #20) Opened
schools_affected: Sprague Middle School (Middle School #20)
description: New $66.9 million three-story middle school opened at 10611 Mason Road in the educational village housing Bridgeland High School and Wells Elementary. Named after a 26-year CFISD veteran.

title: Elementary School #59 (Miramesa) Opened
schools_affected: Elementary #59 (in Miramesa subdivision)
description: New elementary school opened at West Road and Miramesa Drive, designed with connected library and cafeteria. This was the final new school in the 2019 bond program.

title: Major Redistricting Affecting 44 Campuses
schools_affected: Up to 44 campuses, including Cypress Ranch HS, Cypress Falls HS, Bridgeland HS, Langham Creek HS, and dozens of elementary/middle schools
description: Board approved sweeping attendance boundary changes in a contentious 4-3 vote to populate three new campuses and relieve overcrowding (Smith MS at 134% capacity, multiple elementary schools at 118%). Over 5,500 community feedback forms were submitted. The Stone Gate neighborhood controversy over the Cypress Ranch-to-Cypress Falls shift was particularly heated.

title: New Administration Building and Transportation Center
schools_affected: District operations
description: Mark Henry, Ed.D. Administration Building (MHAB) opened in 2023, named after the retiring superintendent. Transportation Center #6 opened near Cypress Woods HS for $26.8M, including bus parking, fueling, and training facilities.

title: Kallison Ranch Area Middle School Opened
schools_affected: Kallison Ranch Area Middle School (new campus)
description: $57 million new middle school opened in fall 2021, funded by the 2018 bond ($848.9M). Located in the rapidly growing far west Bexar County area.

title: Village at WestPointe North Elementary Opened
schools_affected: Village at WestPointe North Area Elementary (new campus)
description: $35 million new elementary school opened in fall 2021, funded by the 2018 bond. Serving growth in the WestPointe master-planned community.

title: Sonia M. Sotomayor High School Opened
schools_affected: Sotomayor High School (NISD's 12th high school)
description: $152.5 million new high school (the Galm Area HS project) opened, named after Supreme Court Justice Sonia Sotomayor. It is the 12th and newest high school in the district. Opened without a senior class.

title: $992 Million Bond Approved
schools_affected: 81 elementary schools (renovations), 1 new elementary school, district-wide infrastructure
description: NISD voters approved a record $992M bond. A major shift from prior growth-focused bonds: $645.5M went to renovations at 81 elementary schools (classrooms, CTE, fine arts, athletics, libraries, playgrounds); $207.3M for infrastructure upgrades; $45M for one new elementary school (Village at WestPointe West area); $23.7M for a baseball/softball complex near Sotomayor HS.

title: FM 471 North Area Elementary (#4) Opened
schools_affected: New elementary school (FM 471 North area)
description: $35.8 million new elementary school, the last new school funded by the 2018 bond, opened in fall 2023.

title: Chumbley Elementary Opened + Boundary Changes
schools_affected: Chumbley Elementary (new), Cole Elementary, Galm Elementary
description: New $45M elementary school (funded by 2022 bond) opened in far west Bexar County in the Riverstone at WestPointe subdivision. Named "Chumbley Elementary." Boundary changes approved Nov. 14, 2023, affecting Cole ES and Galm ES to populate the new school and relieve overcrowding at Cole.

title: Colonies North Elementary Renovation
schools_affected: Colonies North Elementary
description: $35 million renovation to replace the cafeteria, gymnasium, and several classrooms at this aging campus, funded by the 2022 bond. Board approved the design in December 2023.

title: School Board Redistricting
schools_affected: Governance (7 single-member trustee districts)
description: NISD trustees adopted a new map for single-member trustee districts after 2020 Census data showed a 77.5% population differential between the most and least populous districts (far exceeding the 10% threshold). The new map reduced the differential to 6.7%.

title: $1.26 Billion Bond Approved
schools_affected: District-wide (new schools, renovations, technology, natatorium)
description: All three propositions passed: Prop A (65.66%), Prop B (66.62%), Prop C (56.67%). Funds construction of new schools, safety/security improvements, technology upgrades, and a natatorium. Includes a $223M rebuild of Clements High School (foundation had shifted) and a new elementary school in Harvest Green.

title: Bond Program $165 Million Shortfall
schools_affected: Harvest Green ES (eliminated), transportation facility (deferred), fine arts/athletics projects (reduced)
description: Shortly after projects began, a $165M deficit was discovered in the $1.26B bond program. Investigation showed district leaders failed to adjust costs for inflation when the bond was delayed from Nov 2022 to May 2023. On Oct. 21, 2024, trustees voted to eliminate the new Harvest Green elementary school ($47.6M), defer a transportation facility, and reduce fine arts/athletics projects.

title: Amy Coleman Middle School Construction
schools_affected: Amy Coleman Middle School (MS #16, new campus in Fresno area)
