description: A 235,325 sq ft, two-story facility with two gymnasiums, two football fields, and four tennis courts. Named after the district's first Black female principal. Bond-funded. Will rebalance enrollment from two existing middle schools.

date: December 2025 (draft plans released); decision expected March 2026
title: Proposed Closure of 7 Elementary Schools + Redistricting
schools_affected: Austin Parkway ES, Dulles ES, Fleming ES, Glover ES, Mission West ES, Ridgegate ES, Sugar Mill ES
description: Draft boundary plans propose closing 7 of 52 elementary schools (all under 600 students, utilization 40-77%) as part of district-wide boundary changes tied to the new Amy Coleman MS opening. Community opposition is strong, especially around A-rated Sugar Mill ES. Final board vote expected March 2026.

title: New Campuses Opened (2025 Bond Projects)
schools_affected: Multiple new campuses (part of 2023 bond)
description: Fort Bend ISD opened new school campuses as part of the ongoing $1.26B bond program implementation. These include bond-funded facilities in the growing Fresno and Missouri City areas.

title: $2.44 Billion Bond Approved
schools_affected: 25 campuses for modernization; district-wide safety/HVAC/technology
description: Austin voters approved the largest bond in the district's history across three propositions: Prop A ($2.316B for facility upgrades/modernization of 25 schools), Prop B ($75.5M for technology), Prop C ($47.4M for athletic facilities). Projects range from complete campus rebuilds to partial renovations, prioritizing Title 1 schools.

title: Odom Elementary Renovation Kickoff
schools_affected: Odom Elementary (built 1970)
description: First "construction kickoff" for the 2022 bond program. Renovation includes a new secured front entry, new small group meeting spaces, and enclosure of open-concept classrooms built without doors or full walls.

title: Wooten Elementary Full Modernization
schools_affected: Wooten Elementary
description: Became the first full modernization unveiled from the $2.4B bond package. Described as "safe, functional, and inspiring," it represents the template for 24 additional modernization projects.

title: 10 School Closures Approved (Consolidation Plan)
schools_affected: 8 elementary schools (Barrington, Becker, Dawson, Oak Springs, Ridgetop, Sunset Valley, Widen, Winn Montessori) and 2 middle schools (Bedichek, Martin). International High School also closing.
description: Facing a $19.7M budget deficit and potential TEA takeover (three middle schools had 4 consecutive F ratings), the board approved closing 10 schools, reassigning 3,796 students and eliminating 6,319 seats, saving $21.5M annually. Three schools originally on the list (Bryker Woods, Maplewood, Palm) were removed. Superintendent Segura indicated more closures and boundary changes will follow.

title: International High School Closure
schools_affected: International High School
description: This specialized school serving immigrants transitioning to Texas public education will close due to persistently low enrollment.

title: Future Boundary Changes and Additional Consolidations Planned
schools_affected: District-wide
description: AISD announced that district-wide boundary changes and additional school consolidations will be brought to trustees in the future to balance enrollment. Some trustees warned budget issues could lead to more closures.

schools_affected: Humes Middle School
description: Humes Middle School, a former Achievement School District charter school, closed at the end of the 2023-24 school year after the district denied its charter renewal application. Students were redirected to Booker T. Washington Middle and High School. The building is under consideration for reuse by nonprofit New Ballet as an arts-focused school.

schools_affected: ASD Charter School 1 (Frayser Community Schools); ASD Charter School 2; ASD Charter School 3; ASD Charter School 4
description: Four Achievement School District charter schools closed when their charter contracts expired in summer 2024 after the MSCS board denied renewal applications. Five ASD charter schools had faced uncertain futures; the board approved only two charter applications for 2024-25 while denying seven others. The ASD model was widely acknowledged as a failure by Tennessee lawmakers.

schools_affected: Georgian Hills Elementary; 3 additional schools (names pending board vote)
description: MSCS leaders recommended closing four schools and transferring one to a neighboring suburban district by end of academic year 2025-26. Schools in Northwest and Southwest regions were chosen due to underenrollment and high deferred maintenance. The district faces over $1.6 billion in building repairs over the next decade, with 10 buildings reaching end of useful life. Eight MSCS schools enrolled fewer than 150 students in 2023-24.

schools_affected: Up to 15 schools by 2028 (10 additional beyond first 5)
description: Long-term facilities plan released December 2025 calls for closing up to 15 schools by 2028. Five already recommended for 2026 closure. Remaining 10 closures planned for 2027-2028, mostly in Northwest and Southwest regions with the most chronically underenrolled and oldest buildings. The ad hoc facilities committee recommended asking Shelby County Commission for $750 million to fund repairs and closures over 10 years.

schools_affected: New Cordova Area High School; New Frayser High School
description: MSCS asked Shelby County for over $200 million for construction of two new high schools -- one in Cordova area (construction began mid-2024, target completion fall 2026) and one for Frayser community. The Cordova school replaces capacity lost from state-mandated transfer of Germantown schools (3G schools). The board approved land purchase in February 2023. This will be the district's first new high school in over a decade.

schools_affected: Buena Vista Elementary; Robert E. Lillard Elementary; Joelton Middle; Cohn Learning Center
description: Nashville school board unanimously voted to close four schools under the ReimaginED consolidation plan, saving an estimated $3.4 million annually. Closures driven by declining enrollment due to school choice and charter school expansion. At Buena Vista, 62.4% of zoned students exercised school choice (39% to charters, 61% to other district schools).

schools_affected: Percy Priest Elementary (new $42.3M building); Lakeview Elementary (new $41.7M building); Paragon Mills Elementary (new $36.4M building)
description: Three new replacement elementary school buildings opened for the 2025-26 school year totaling over $120M in investment. Percy Priest (800 students, Pre-K-5) at 1700 Otter Creek Road features new gymnasium, larger cafeteria, wireless projectors. Lakeview (811 students) in Antioch features state-of- the-art technology. Paragon Mills also rebuilt on existing campus. Districts served saw 12-18% population growth from 2010-2020.

schools_affected: Julia Green Elementary (rezoned to Percy Priest); Antioch cluster schools; Glencliff cluster schools; Hillsboro cluster schools
description: For 2025-26, MNPS proposed rezoning changes for Antioch, Glencliff, and Hillsboro clusters related to new school openings. A portion of Julia Green zone rezoned to new Percy Priest Elementary (approx. 28 students affected). Ida B. Wells students to be rezoned to Jere Baxter Middle and Maplewood High beginning 2026-27 to eliminate split feeder pattern.

schools_affected: Columbus Alternative High School; Buckeye Middle School; Broadleigh Elementary; Moler Elementary; West Broad Elementary
description: Columbus Board of Education voted to close five schools after months of debate. Combined, they enroll over 2,000 students and employ over 120 teachers. Closures driven by enrollment at less than half of peak levels (from 110K to ~47K). A 28-member facilities task force initially considered 20 schools; the board spared North Linden and Lindbergh. West Broad closure contingent on funding for replacement. District downtown offices at 270 E. State St. also closed, consolidating to South Side building. Earliest closures take effect 2026.

schools_affected: Duxberry Park Arts Impact Elementary; Fairwood Alternative Elementary; Como Elementary; Columbus Gifted Academy (former Everett Middle)
description: As part of $50.4 million in budget cuts, the Columbus Board of Education voted to close four additional schools and eliminate numerous staff positions. Ohio public schools face $2 billion in state funding cuts over two years. The district teachers union issued a scathing statement saying the board "should feel shame."

schools_affected: Brown Street Academy; Clarke Street Academy; Siefert School; Starms Discovery Learning Center; Auer Avenue School; Hopkins Lloyd Community School; Jackson Elementary School; Dr. George Washington Carver Academy; Oliver Wendell Holmes School; Andrew S. Douglas Middle School; Keefe Avenue School; Robert M. LaFollette School; William T. Sherman School
description: MPS identified 13 schools for potential closure or merger as part of a long-range facilities plan developed with consultant Perkins Eastman. Enrollment down 32% over 20 years (from 100K+ to ~65K). Buildings average 80+ years old. Criteria: enrollment less than 50% of capacity, declining enrollment over 5 years, less than 1 mile from another underenrolled school. 36 schools below 70% capacity, 14 schools less than half-full. Closures not planned until 2027-28 school year. MPS superintendent said "much more than 5" schools will eventually close or merge.

Milwaukee voters narrowly approved a $252 million school referendum to support operations and facilities. The vote came as the district faces severe financial pressure from declining enrollment and aging infrastructure. Over three decades, building count decreased only 3.9% despite a 29.1% drop in enrollment.

schools_affected: Francis Bellamy PreK Center; Floro Torrence School 83; Paul Miller School 114; Raymond Brandes School 65; George Buck School 94; Francis Parker Montessori School 56
description: Under the Rebuilding Stronger plan unanimously approved by the IPS board, six school buildings closed at end of 2022-23 school year, displacing over 1,200 students and 300 staff. Driven by enrollment decline from 27,988 in 2015-16 to 19,596 in 2022-23 in traditional schools. Four buildings assigned reuse plans including partnership with Indiana School for the Blind. District also reconfigured grades, expanded IB/Montessori/dual language programs, and created standalone middle schools.

schools_affected: Broad Ripple Middle School (in former Broad Ripple High School building)
description: As part of Rebuilding Stronger, the former Broad Ripple High School building (closed 2017) reopened as Broad Ripple Middle School serving grades 6-8. This reflects IPS strategy of repurposing closed buildings while implementing grade reconfigurations and four enrollment zones.

schools_affected: 50 IPS schools (proposed charter conversion)
description: House Bill 1136 proposed converting 50 IPS schools to charter schools and dissolving the district, along with Gary Community Schools and three other districts, because more than 50% of students residing in their boundaries attend non-district schools. A separate bill would change control over school closures and buildings. IPS enrollment: 31,300 total (21,000 in district-managed schools). Indianapolis has ~9,000 more seats than enrolled students across IPS and charter schools.

schools_affected: Potentially 20-30 schools (no specific schools named yet)
description: MPS board passed a "transformation resolution" directing the district to account for physical space. District built for 45,000 students had only 28,500 enrolled. 52% of buildings underutilized. Of 55,129 school-aged children in Minneapolis, only 28,255 (51%) enrolled in MPS. Superintendent Sayles-Adams asked to provide closure/consolidation recommendations by April 2026. Budget gap projected at $84.3 million for FY2026. The district expected to run out of reserve funds during 2025-26 school year.

schools_affected: Galtier Elementary; Jackson Elementary; John A. Johnson Elementary; Parkway Elementary; L'Etoile du Nord Lower Campus
description: St. Paul school board voted 5-2 in December 2021 to close five schools by June 2022, displacing approximately 2,040 students. Closures driven by declining enrollment and excess of 8,000 empty seats. LEAP High School, Wellstone, and Highwood Hills were spared after vocal opposition. Aimed to create larger, more well-rounded schools with greater appeal to parents.

schools_affected: Barack and Michelle Obama Elementary
description: As part of the December 2021 board vote, Barack and Michelle Obama Elementary closed at end of 2022-23 school year. Cherokee Heights Montessori merged into JJ Hill Montessori; JJ Hill later planned to relocate to the renovated Obama building in 2024 or 2025.

SPPS reported a $107 million budget deficit heading into 2024-25 school year, the largest in district history. Plans to cut afterschool programs, custodial, food service and support staff. Superintendent Joe Gothard stated "the cuts we are facing are larger than we've ever faced before."

district: East Baton Rouge Parish School System
schools_affected: Bernard Terrace Elementary; Eva Legard Center; Ryan Elementary; Westminster Elementary; Capitol Middle; Winbourne Elementary; J.K. Haynes Elementary; IDEA Public Schools charter (2 campuses)
description: EBR Parish School Board unanimously approved (7-0) a sweeping realignment plan closing 9 schools, relocating 4, reconfiguring 7 grade structures, and redrawing 12 attendance zones. Over 10,000 students and 1,400+ staff affected. The district has capacity for 60,000+ students but educates fewer than 40,000, with 20,000 excess seats. The closures remove nearly half of the district's F-rated schools and three D-rated schools. Superintendent LaMont Cole led the effort in his ninth month.

district: East Baton Rouge Parish School System
schools_affected: Melrose Elementary (to K-2 foundational learning center); Merrydale Elementary (to K-2 foundational learning center); Capitol Elementary (to grades 3-6); Glen Oaks Park Elementary (to grades 3-5); Scotlandville Middle (expansion from 200 to 400 students); Capitol High (moved to Capitol Middle site, grades 7-12)
description: As part of the realignment, multiple schools received new grade configurations. Melrose and Merrydale become K-2 "foundational learning centers" with two teachers per classroom. Capitol and Glen Oaks Park shift to upper elementary grades. Scotlandville Middle doubles capacity. Capitol High relocates to Capitol Middle site as a 7-12 school.

schools_affected: Grace King High School (closed, students to Bonnabel & Riverdale); Gretna Middle School (closed, students to Marrero Middle); Haynes Academy (relocated to Grace King site); Thomas Jefferson Academy (relocated to Gretna Middle site); St. Ville Elementary (students to Woodmere while new school built)
description: Jefferson Parish School Board approved consolidating 7 schools, relocating 2 schools, creating 1 new Pre-K-8 school, and planning 2 new campuses as part of an infrastructure and efficiency plan. Grace King HS and Gretna MS absorbed into nearby schools. The closing schools showed lower scores than the year before, among the lowest in the district. Part of effort to address declining enrollment and shift students from aging buildings.

schools_affected: New St. Ville Elementary (under construction at existing site); Second new campus (planned)
description: Jefferson Parish in final stages of designing two new $48 million schools. St. Ville Elementary students temporarily absorbed into Woodmere Elementary while new school built at current St. Ville site. Superintendent James Gray said no additional consolidations planned for 2024, but more likely "near-term."

schools_affected: Six charter schools consolidated into three
description: Charter leaders consolidated six schools into three schools in summer 2023, following voluntary closure of two under-enrolled schools in summer 2022. Since 2018-19, NOLA-PS has closed or changed operators at 14+ low-performing charter schools. 21 schools (one in four New Orleans charters) faced high-stakes renewal decisions in fall 2023.

As of October 2024, 47,667 students enrolled in 70 NOLA Public Schools, reflecting continued post-pandemic decline. District facing potential $49 million budget shortfall driven by too many empty seats. "The budget issue would not be as bad if we were fully enrolled," said FirstLine Schools CEO. Further campus closures expected.

schools_affected: University High School (new $153M building planned); Hawthorne Avenue Elementary (relocated to existing University HS building)
description: NJ Schools Development Authority to spend $153 million to build a new South Ward high school (University High School) and relocate Hawthorne Avenue Elementary students to the existing HS building, with demolition of the old Hawthorne Ave building. Part of state plan to replace 13 of Newark's 33 school buildings built before 1920 (20 still need replacement). District estimated $2 billion needed for full repairs.

State Sen. Vin Gopal drafting legislation to mandate consolidation of some of NJ's 590+ school districts, particularly those with fewer than 500 students. NJ has the highest property taxes in the country with school taxes accounting for 52% of local property taxes ($15B in school aid = 25% of state spending). Henry Hudson Regional merger (Highlands + Atlantic Highlands, 2023 referendum) cited as success model.

schools_affected: 24 new school buildings (11,010 new seats)
description: Mayor Adams and SCA opened 24 new school buildings for 2024-25 school year -- the most new K-12 seats since 2003. Distribution: 9 in Brooklyn, 8 in Bronx, 1 in Manhattan, 6 in Queens. Features include modern classrooms, advanced technology, green spaces. Addresses overcrowding and state-mandated smaller class sizes. In addition to 20,000+ seats added earlier in Adams administration. 2025-29 Capital Plan funds another 33,417 seats.

schools_affected: 13 school mergers/grade removals approved in 2024 (most since 2018)
description: NYC quietly accelerated school mergers as enrollment dropped. Over past six years, 35 proposals to merge, close, or remove grades from schools passed. 13 approved in 2024 alone (the most in any year since at least 2018). Roughly two-thirds of affected schools in Brooklyn or Bronx. Schools affected had higher proportions of Black, Latino, and low-income students than the median city school.

schools_affected: M.S. 394 (17K394) in Crown Heights
description: Panel for Educational Policy voted to close M.S. 394, a Pre-K-8 school in Crown Heights, phased out over three school years. Only the third closure approved under Mayor Adams. A new Central Brooklyn Literacy Academy (for students with dyslexia) will open in the same building -- the second city-operated school designed for reading challenges.

schools_affected: 112 schools with fewer than 150 students (up from 80 two years ago); 190 schools with fewer than 200 students (up from 81 in 2016)
description: NYC K-12 enrollment fell ~130,000 students (14%) since fall 2016. As of Oct 2025, 884,400 students enrolled, down 22,000 (2.4%) year-over-year. Nearly two-thirds of ~1,600 schools had fewer students than projected. SCA projects enrollment will fall 200,000+ (26%) over next decade. Immigration slowdown under federal enforcement has sharply reduced migrant enrollment that previously offset declines.

NATIONAL ENROLLMENT DECLINE: Public school enrollment decreased 2.5% from 2019-2023, with NCES projecting loss of another 2.7 million students by 2031-32. Operating schools decreased from 99,297 (2023-24) to 99,073 (2024-25). Factors include record-low birth rates, shift to charter schools (2.1M to 3.7M students 2011-2021), homeschooling 56% higher than pre- pandemic, and declining public satisfaction (12 percentage point drop 2019-2025).

BELLWETHER ANALYSIS - SYSTEMS UNDER STRAIN: Among 9,500 school systems studied, 68% experienced enrollment declines between 2019-20 and 2023-24, representing loss of ~2 million students. Yet fewer than 1% of schools closed. West (76%) and Northeast (73%) had highest share of declining districts. "Hold harmless" state funding and federal pandemic relief delayed closures, but relief funds expired September 2025, likely triggering surge in closures.

THOUSANDS AT RISK: Youth Today/The 74 exclusive data showed thousands of schools at risk of closing due to enrollment loss. Schools with majority- Black student bodies were about three times as likely to close as schools with smaller proportions of Black students (2000-2018). California has 1,400+ schools where enrollment dropped at least 20% during pandemic.

California voters passed Proposition 2, a $10 billion state bond for school construction -- the first since 2016. Passed with 56.8% support. A record 252 school districts asked voters to pass local bonds totaling $40 billion. Notable approvals: $9 billion in LAUSD, $900 million in Pasadena Unified, $1.15 billion in San Jose Unified.

schools_affected: Shaw Elementary (Dorchester) merged with Taylor (Mattapan) - Sept 2024; Sumner Elementary (Roslindale) merged with Philbrick - Sept 2025
description: Boston School Committee voted 6-0 to approve mergers of two pairs of elementary schools, affecting nearly 1,200 students. Small schools targeted lacked basic amenities like gyms, cafeterias, and libraries. District leaders had unveiled a long-term facilities plan noting as many as half the city's public schools could close as enrollment dropped 14%+ in past decade. Critics raised concerns about disproportionate impact on Black and Latino students.

schools_affected: New Highland Academy + RISE Community School merged into Highland Community School; 10+ additional schools planned for consolidation
description: OUSD board voted on budget cuts including layoffs and consolidation of at least 10 schools beginning 2024-25 school year. In 2023, New Highland Academy and RISE Community School merged to form Highland Community School. Ongoing financial challenges and enrollment decline driving further consolidation.

schools_affected: Multiple schools under Resource Alignment Initiative
description: SFUSD launched Resource Alignment Initiative to address portfolio of schools where resources are "stretched too thin across too many sites." Enrollment declined 4,000 since 2012-13 with projected additional 4,600 decline by 2032. Process includes potential school mergers, co-locations, and closures.

Vermont, the most rural state, lost ~20% of K-12 enrollment in two decades. Lawmakers pushing to reorganize 118 school districts (ranging 200-4,000 students) into larger systems of 4,000-8,000 students each. In 2024, Vermonters facing double-digit property tax increases rejected nearly one-third of school budgets.

At least 10 states considered measures to mandate or incentivize district mergers in the past three years. States include New Jersey, Vermont, South Carolina, Indiana, and others. Driven by declining enrollment, rising per-pupil costs, and property tax pressure. Opponents argue evidence that consolidation saves money or helps students is mixed.
